analysis.one_liner: Restores cut Social Security benefits for post-1979 retirees and lifts the payroll tax cap on high earnings.
analysis.headline: A bill to recompute lower Social Security benefits for post-1979 retirees and remove the payroll tax cap on high earners died in a House subcommittee with zero cosponsors and no votes.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would fix the "notch" problem, in which people who became eligible for Social Security in or after 1979 received smaller checks than earlier retirees because of a 1977 formula change, by recomputing their benefits under the old rules and paying retroactive lump sums. It would also repeal the ceiling on wages subject to Social Security payroll taxes, so that high earners would pay Social Security tax on every dollar of wages and self-employment income instead of only up to an annual cap. The bill never received a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Retirees, survivors, and disabled beneficiaries whose benefits were computed under the post-1977 formula, especially those with long pre-1979 work records, would get higher monthly checks and retroactive lump-sum payments. Workers earning below the annual wage cap would be unaffected directly, but the system's finances would shift toward upper earners, who would pay Social Security tax on their full income.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Post-1979 Social Security retirees and beneficiaries

how_it_helps.text: Recomputes the benefits of people who became eligible in or after 1979 under the pre-1979 rules, restoring the higher benefit levels earlier retirees received and paying each affected beneficiary a lump sum covering the shortfall since their benefits began.

Removes the annual cap on wages and self-employment income subject to Social Security taxes, so high earners pay Social Security tax on all their earnings, and their full earnings also count toward benefit calculations.
Makes the tax change effective for wages paid and self-employment income earned after December 1989, so the additional revenue would begin flowing to the trust funds the following year.

analysis.who_pays: High earners above the Social Security wage cap would pay Social Security tax on their entire wages and self-employment income, and their employers would pay the matching share on those wages too, raising the cost of employing high-paid workers. The government would also owe one-time lump-sum payments to recomputed beneficiaries and somewhat higher ongoing benefits, since high earners' full earnings would count toward their benefit formulas.

drawbacks.text: Removing the cap cuts both ways: because the bill also counts high earners' full wages toward their benefit formulas, some of the new tax revenue would be returned to them as higher Social Security benefits, reducing the net savings to the system.
Employers would owe the matching payroll tax on all wages, which raises the cost of employing highly paid workers and could pressure pay or hiring at the top of the wage scale.
The retroactive lump-sum recomputations would create a large one-time payment obligation, and the bill was never costed because no hearing or estimate was ever produced.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit side is concrete and targeted: a specific group of retirees with lower-than-promised checks would be made whole, with back pay. The cost side falls on the highest earners and their employers through an uncapped payroll tax, which is progressive by design, though the bill's own text gives some of that money back to high earners as higher benefits, making it less of a pure revenue raiser than it first appears. A real fix probably would have phased the retroactive payments to manage the one-time cost. The larger failure is procedural: with zero cosponsors and no hearing, the bill was never examined or debated at all, so the public never got an honest accounting of what it would cost or save.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Ways and Means Subcommittee on Social Security three days after introduction and sat there until the Congress ended, with no hearing, no markup, and no vote.

narrative.text: Representative Bruce Morrison introduced the bill on May 16, 1989, and it was referred the same day to the House Ways and Means Committee.

On May 19, 1989, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Social Security, which is where the record ends; the bill attracted no cosponsors and received no further action before the 101st Congress expired on January 3, 1991.
No member of either party signed on as a cosponsor at any point during the two-year Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High earners kept paying Social Security tax only up to the annual wage cap, and their employers avoided the matching share on earnings above it, while the retirees shortchanged by the 1977 formula change never received the higher benefits or back pay.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High earners who kept the payroll tax cap

for.name: Rep. Bruce Morrison
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and made the case for fixing the post-1979 benefit disparity and lifting the payroll tax cap.

against.name: Subcommittee on Social Security, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after its May 19, 1989 referral and never held a hearing or reported it out.

against.name: Dan Rostenkowski
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: As chairman of the committee of referral, never brought the bill to a markup or the House floor during the two years it was pending.

sides.party_line_note: There were no votes and no cosponsors of either party, so the bill never revealed whether support would have split along party lines.

industries.industry: High-income wage earners above the Social Security cap
industries.note: They would have paid Social Security tax on all wages instead of only up to the annual cap, though the bill also counts those wages toward higher future benefits. Keeping the cap in place preserves their savings.
Employers match the employee payroll tax, so an uncapped base means a matching tax on every high salary, raising the cost of top-end compensation.
The bill repeals the rules that let pension plans integrate with Social Security, a technique employers use to lower their pension contributions, so plan sponsors would owe more in promised benefits.
